RUV achieves mean verification accuracies of $98.9\%$ and $94.9\%$, while rejecting $99.5\%$ and $99.8\%$ of the corresponding ODR submissions.

items.title: Stagewise Adaptive Boosting
items.description: Stagewise algorithms and sparsity-inducing regularization are two influential approaches to high-dimensional modeling. Existing stagewise theory, however, largely centers on convex regularization, whereas stronger sparsity and other structural preferences are often pursued through fixed-level nonconvex optimization rather than generating an entire adaptive solution path. We develop stagewise adaptive boosting, a general framework that builds a monotone path by selecting the update consistent with structural preference. The framework can encourage sparsity along the path itself and also admits extensions that promote other properties of the solution, including group selection, similarity across models for multiple outcomes, and known priorities or prerequisite relations among predictors. We study its theoretical property as well as finite sample performance using simulations and real-data analyses. Across these studies, the proposed pathwise approach often achieves predictive performance comparable to commonly used baselines while selecting substantially smaller models. These results suggest that adaptive stagewise learning provides a practical route to stronger sparsity and richer structural control without repeatedly solving separate weighted or nonconvex optimization problems.

items.title: VidEngram: Agentic Long-Term Video Understanding via Structured Hierarchical Memory
items.description: Long-video question answering is wasteful and lossy when a multimodal model must re-encode the same video for every query: context limits force sparse sampling or truncation, and no reusable representation remains for later questions. We present VidEngram, an agentic video QA system that builds a persistent hierarchical memory once at ingest and answers later questions from that memory. VidEngram captions video and audio jointly with Qwen2.5-Omni, consolidates segment memories into episode and entity layers, and uses a text-only agentic planner with specialized retrieval tools to produce grounded answers. The web interface makes this process inspectable: users can watch memory formation, inspect retrieval traces, verify cited evidence in the video player, and explore entity relationships. On the full OmniVideoBench, VidEngram with a GPT-5-mini planner outperforms a strong single-pass Qwen2.5-Omni baseline (37.0% vs. 32.3%), with gains concentrated on longer videos where single-pass coverage becomes sparse. Because perception is paid once, subsequent queries use low-cost text-only planning.

items.title: ReMoVe: Refining a Video Model's Own Motion for Coherent Human Video Generation
items.description: Video generation models have become increasingly capable of synthesizing realistic human motion, yet they often lose track of the very structure that makes the motion plausible. As generated human motion becomes more complex, videos can suffer from progressive body deformation and appearance drift across frames. Existing motion-controlled methods use explicit representations to stabilize generation, but typically rely on pre-defined motion sequences as references. This raises a fundamental question: if the base generator already produces a usable coarse motion, why replace it with an external one? ReMoVe answers this question by treating the coarse output as a motion hypothesis rather than a final result. ReMoVe recovers and refines the underlying motion, then renders the refined motion as 3D mesh and transfers facial appearance onto it, thereby improving motion accuracy and identity consistency. We further derive depth from the same 3D scene and camera trajectory to impose scene-level spatial consistency beyond the mesh. By jointly conditioning video generation models on mesh and depth, ReMoVe synthesizes high-quality motion videos with controllable camera trajectories and enhanced spatio-temporal consistency. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ReMoVe improves human structural stability, appearance consistency, temporal coherence, and motion-following fidelity, while retaining the base generator's motion prior and offering accurate camera control.

items.title: Speaking-Clock Mamba: Phoneme-Conditioned State-Space Modeling for Visual Forced Alignment
items.description: Visual forced alignment (VFA) locates phoneme and word boundaries in a silent talking-face video given its transcript. Existing methods mainly enforce transcript order at the decoding stage, leaving the encoder without an explicit mechanism to anchor its temporally evolving representation to transcript progress. As a result, phoneme-specific evidence is blurred and alignment drift accumulates over long sequences. In this paper, we propose Speaking-Clock Mamba, which makes transcript progress part of the temporal recurrence. A selective state-space (Mamba) backbone is inserted between the visual frontend and the Conformer cross-attention encoder, and a Phoneme-Conditioned Selective Scan (PCSS) conditions its input-dependent step size on a supervised, structurally monotone speaking clock that estimates progress through the transcript. Since causal and bidirectional variants of this backbone make complementary errors, a training-free selector picks the more confident alignment per utterance. Experiments on LRS2 and LRS3 show consistent gains over protocol-matched baselines, and the supervised clock provides an explicit estimate of alignment progress.

items.title: UMM-JEPA: Generative Pretraining via Masked Next-Scale Representation Prediction for Unified Multimodal Models
items.description: Unified multimodal models can support both visual understanding and generation, yet generative training does not necessarily improve understanding. We argue that this limitation may arise from a mismatch between the representation targeted by generation and the perceptual representation used for understanding. Conventional generation objectives primarily optimize synthesis-oriented spaces such as discrete visual codes or generative latents. We therefore introduce UMM-JEPA, which reformulates generation as progressive prediction of continuous visual-understanding representations. The model constructs a multi-scale representation hierarchy from coarse to fine, while pixel rendering is decoupled from representation pretraining and attached only afterward. Controlled comparisons show that the representation-prediction objective accounts for most of the understanding improvement, while a data-matched control leaves the group means nearly unchanged. UMM-JEPA reaches a 16-benchmark visual mean of 51.71, against 46.36 for the understanding-only Qwen-VL baseline, and the text mean also rises. Compared with discrete-code and latent-flow generation objectives, perceptual representation prediction yields stronger and more consistent transfer to understanding. Linear probes and visual-evidence interventions further reveal richer object and spatial structure and stronger use of image-specific information. These results suggest that generation can benefit understanding when it directly supervises the perceptual representations that understanding consumes.

items.title: LogicEye: Agent Driven Multimodal Dataset for Interpretable Ophthalmic Diagnosis
items.description: Clinical adoption of ophthalmic Artificial Intelligence remains limited by low interpretability and a lack of finely annotated multimodal data. Most existing datasets provide only coarse disease labels without the granular pathological findings required for differential diagnosis. We present LogicEye$^{Agent}$, a dual-pool inference and verification agent that emulates clinical reasoning by jointly verifying positive inclusion signs and negative exclusion criteria. Using LogicEye$^{Agent}$, we curate LogicEye$^{Data}$, a large-scale multimodal dataset of 804,461 fundus and OCT images paired with structured pathological reports spanning 38 diseases and 29 subtypes, with quality assured through joint verification by multimodal large language models and clinical experts. Building on this dataset, we further develop LogicEye$^{Bench}$, which incorporates a category-constrained loss for hierarchical disease recognition and report generation. Grounding coarse labels into verified visual findings effectively curtails diagnostic hallucinations and establishes a solid foundation for interpretable vision-language modeling in ophthalmology. The code is available at:https://github.com/Eden35/LogicEye-Agent-Driven-Multimodal-Dataset-for-Interpretable-Ophthalmic-Diagnosis.

items.title: Evidence-Calibrated Selective Decoding for Reliable Visual Question Answering
items.description: Visual question answering systems can produce confident responses that are weakly supported by their input images. Contrastive decoding can reduce this dependence on language priors, but a fixed correction may also overturn a correct answer, while selective answering can conceal errors by reducing coverage. We develop evidence-calibrated selective decoding, a framework that separates three decisions: whether local visual evidence supports a candidate, how strongly to correct the original distribution, and whether the resulting answer should be released under a verification budget. Evidence Verification across Crops (EVC) measures visual support and disagreement; Adaptive Contrast Correction (ACC) applies a bounded modification within the backbone's plausible candidate set; Budgeted Selective Answering (BSA) calibrates an answer-admission threshold on held-out images. We provide a complete mathematical specification, bounded-perturbation analysis, and an evaluation protocol that distinguishes forced answering from selective risk. Our quantitative analysis re-examines published baselines on POPE instantiated over MSCOCO, A-OKVQA, and GQA, together with four MME subtasks. These public measurements reveal variation across backbones, tasks, and correction settings that motivates adaptive control. The proposed framework has not yet undergone model-level evaluation; its effectiveness remains a falsifiable hypothesis rather than an established empirical result.

items.title: Thinking from Another Side of the Box: Spacetime Images for Computer Vision
items.description: Computer vision methods for video understanding, such as object detection and tracking, inherit the way videos are captured and displayed: as successive frames processed sequentially. However, a video is an inhomogeneous 2D+time volume of pixels, named voxels, and frames are only one family of cuts through it. In this frame-based representation, static backgrounds introduce computational redundancy, and motion can only be understood across several frames. In this position paper, we study another family of cuts: spacetime images (STIs), obtained by sampling any set of pixels other than frames, for instance a line of pixels followed over time. Such images are familiar in narrow forms, from line-scan inspection and kymographs to spatiotemporal slices for motion analysis, but have received little attention as a general input representation for computer vision and are often limited to (x,t) or (y,t) cuts. We define new cuts leading to STIs in their general form, explain how to read their content, and show that a family of cuts tiles the video so that existing dense annotations transfer at no cost. We also detail how motion appears in an STI, spatially and in the frequency domain, and discuss applications such as walking pedestrians, deposited objects, and dynamic scenes. Two pilot experiments illustrate the representation. The first trains a segmentation network entirely in the spacetime domain, on transferred annotations, and performs background subtraction on CDnet 2014 close to supervised frame-based methods, without explicit temporal modeling. The second recovers the pan speed of a camera as a moving cut, identified by a simple criterion on the frequency spectrum of the resulting image, turning a temporal estimation problem into the choice of a cut. Our position is not that STIs should replace frames, but that slicing the video volume is a design variable worth studying in its own right.

items.title: Exists, Valid: Calibrated Validity of Stored 3D Geometry Across Long Observation Gaps
items.description: Repeated airborne LiDAR surveys are costly, while stored 3D geometry can become outdated between observations. Existing change-detection methods compare observed epochs. However, they do not quantify the validity of geometry that has not been revisited. We distinguish observation, existence and geometric validity using a probabilistic filter over five geometric transitions: persistence, modification, growth, removal and replacement. The framework learns class-specific continuous-time transition priors from interval-censored observations and combines shape residuals with LiDAR free-space evidence. Functional anchors enable prior sharing across sites with different survey frequencies. In controlled experiments with misspecified dynamics and 60% visibility, our method reduces combined error from 36.9% to 16.5% and expected calibration error (ECE) from 0.19-0.32 to 0.017. Cross-site sharing reduces ECE at two-survey sites from 0.156 to 0.029. On Urb3DCD-v2, the method achieves 9.8% combined error and 0.016 ECE, outperforming baselines at 12.6% and at least 0.070, respectively. Re-survey prioritisation improves only modestly over random selection with two observations. Code and an evaluation protocol are released at https://github.com/anwaarua/life4d.

items.title: Robust-GCD
items.description: Generalized Category Discovery (GCD) classifies an unlabeled pool that contains both known and novel classes, given labels for the known classes only. Existing GCD methods assume that every un- labeled image is clean, but unlabeled data collected in the wild is often degraded by blur, sensor noise and compression artifacts. We formalize the setting in which an unknown fraction of the unlabeled pool is corrupted by an unknown operator as Degraded Generalized Category Discovery (D-GCD). To tackle it, we propose Robust-GCD, a framework that estimates the corruption directly from the unlabeled pool and uses the estimate to build labeled anchors for known classes and pseudo-anchors for novel classes inside the corrupted region of feature space. A trust curriculum controls how much the unlabeled pool is trusted while the anchors take hold, and a paired alignment loss keeps a clean image and its corrupted twin close in feature space. Across five datasets and multiple corruption families, Robust-GCD recovers between 43% and 96% of the All accuracy that SimGCD loses under contamination, and more than 60% on four of the five datasets, with the largest gains on the corrupted images themselves.

items.title: SynPanZ: A Synthetic Dataset to Improve Multi-Animal Pose Estimation in Chimpanzees (Pan troglodytes)
items.description: Pose estimation underpins a wide range of automated monitoring workflows in animal behaviour research. Unfortunately, endangered great apes such as chimpanzees suffer a chronic shortage of the type of hand-annotated training data that has made robust pose estimation in humans and other model organisms possible. This paper introduces SynPanZ, a synthetically generated dataset for pose estimation in great apes. Our pipeline renders multi-individual scenes from rigged, behaviourally animated chimpanzee models with randomised poses, lighting conditions, environmental contexts, and camera motion, producing animated RGB videos with per-instance 2D keypoint locations without manual labelling. To test whether synthetic augmentation improves cross-dataset generalisation, four DeepLabCut models are trained under matched settings on data sourced from DeepWild with varying real-to-synthetic augmentation ratios. Models are evaluated on ChimpACT, a visually disjoint zoo dataset. We find that augmenting the DeepWild training data with approximately three times as many synthetic frames nearly doubles instance coverage (12.34% to 22.54%) while maintaining keypoint localisation accuracy on detected individuals (PCK@0.20: 49.71% to 52.25%). Synthetic-only training fails, showing that rendered data complements rather than replaces real annotated data. This work represents a step towards reliable pose estimation for great apes.

items.title: Not All Steps Matter: Temporally Adaptive Spectral Control for Concept Removal in Diffusion Models
items.description: As text-to-image diffusion models see widespread deployment, removing unsafe or undesirable concepts without retraining has become a pressing need. Spectral methods are attractive because they are training-free and reversible, yet current variants apply the same output-value (OV) circuit intervention at every denoising step, assuming concept information is temporally uniform. This wastes intervention where concept energy is low while degrading image quality, an inefficiency that compounds across concept types. Through timestep-resolved spectral analysis, concept-specific energy is found to follow a consistent temporal hierarchy: content concepts decay fastest, object concepts are intermediate, and style concepts persist longest. This paper proposes Timestep-Adaptive Spectral Nullification (TASN), which adapts suppression strength and spectral components to the concept energy profile. Cross-attention at each timestep is decomposed into concept-aligned and concept-orthogonal components, and it is proved that when the orthogonal component is approximately stable, the collateral-minimizing schedule sets suppression proportional to concept energy. TASN implements this with a timestep-adaptive spectral subset tracking only active concept directions, strictly generalizing uniform Spectral Nullification (SN). On five red-teaming benchmarks, TASN lowers attack success rate below uniform SN while recovering the majority of its quality loss; ablations confirm gains arise from temporal targeting rather than reduced suppression, generalizing across concept categories and architectures.

items.title: Shared Mobile AR Without Depth Sensors from Monocular Point Maps
items.description: Depth-aware augmented reality on phones needs dense geometry of the surrounding room. iPhones and iPads without LiDAR expose only sparse feature points and detected planes, and ARKit often takes tens of seconds to report the first wall. We describe a scan-free pipeline for these devices. A point-map network (MoGe-2) predicts metric geometry from each camera frame, the remaining depth shift is recovered from the camera intrinsics, and each frame's scale is aligned to views already in the map. A persistent voxel map with visibility-based expiry answers occlusion and collision queries. Co-located devices share one coordinate frame by solving yaw and floor-plane translation from sightings of each other. We evaluate the deployed system on 309 device-sessions from 19 device models without LiDAR, with 179 device-sessions from LiDAR phones in the same deployment as a reference population. A first dense depth map was recorded within 10 s in 80% of sessions, while ARKit had reported a wall plane by then in 25%. The median session scale was 0.98 against ARKit's wall planes and 1.00 against its camera translation. Scale changed by a median of 9% between nearby frames, against 0.4% with LiDAR, and depth points spread three times as widely around walls. In multi-device sessions, 69% of devices without LiDAR reached a converged shared frame, against 84% of LiDAR phones. The main remaining error is scale that changes from frame to frame.

items.title: Spread Too Thin: How Higher Resolution Dilutes a Vision Transformer's Attention, and a Training-Free Rescaling
items.description: A vision transformer read at a higher resolution than it was trained at spreads each attention row over many more patches, yet every row must still hand out exactly one unit of weight. A law of softmax attention predicts that a growing crowd of bounded scores dilutes the attention on any patch or register whose score stays fixed. The same law gives a remedy that needs no training: multiply every score, the sink's included, by the ratio of the logarithms of the test and training token counts. Given sufficient margins at the training resolution, this keeps the attention on a match when one is present, and on a sink such as a register when none is, though trained models need not meet those margins. We test these predictions in public vision transformers and in controlled models read far above their training token count. Attention spreads as predicted. Registers lose their share, though production models compensate in part, and the rescaling holds the share of DINOv2's registers nearly level. Applied at test time without training, the rescaling recovers part of the lost accuracy in nearly every model, with absolute or rotary positions and with registers, and on images with native detail. The calibrated multiplier rises with the logarithmic ratio on average and varies across models. Its rise is steeper than the square-root rule used in image generators; in controlled models the log ratio is also more accurate, while in the public models the two rules' accuracy difference remains unresolved. The rescaling does not restore the attention a model learned, and why it helps, beyond countering the dilution, remains open.

items.title: PolarGait: Constructing Complementary Views from a Single Human Sketch for Gait Recognition
items.description: Existing multimodal gait recognition methods exploit complementary information by fusing heterogeneous representations. Whether useful complementarity can be constructed from a single representation before fusion remains less explored. We propose PolarGait, which constructs complementary views of Human Sketch through filtering and spatial reparameterization. Filter-Oriented Sketch Decomposition (FOSD) uses Gaussian smoothing to extract coherent structures and absolute residuals to capture local response differences. Gait-Oriented Polar Transformation (GOPT) combines silhouette-guided sketch normalization, a gait-oriented center, and lower-body-biased non-uniform angular sampling to construct a polar view complementary to the Cartesian representation. Silhouette provides auxiliary global body-shape information. Experiments on CCPG, SUSTech1K, CASIA-B, and Gait3D validate the framework. Under the single-Sketch setting, FOSD+GOPT improves the original Sketch baseline by 6.6% on CCPG and 4.6% on CASIA-B. The complete PolarGait achieves Rank-1 accuracies of 87.9%, 95.2%, 96.6%, and 86.4% on the four benchmarks, respectively. These results show that complementary gait information can be constructed within a single structured representation and integrated for robust gait recognition.

items.title: ThinkWise: Learning When to Think in Large Multimodal Reasoning Models via Visual and Difficulty Perception
items.description: Large Multimodal Reasoning Models (LMRMs) extend large language models to heterogeneous modalities, demonstrating strong potential across a wide range of open-ended tasks. Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) has been widely adopted to improve reasoning performance in LMRMs; however, existing approaches overlook the critical role of visual perception uncertainty in guiding reasoning processes. We term this limitation Reasoning Allocation Misalignment, where the misalignment between visual perception uncertainty and reasoning depth leads to over-allocation of deep reasoning under uncertain visual grounding, resulting in unnecessarily long reasoning trajectories and degraded performance. To address this issue, we propose ThinkWise, a perception-aware RLVR framework that jointly models task difficulty and visual perception state to regulate reasoning depth. Specifically, we introduce an instance-adaptive visual perception modeling mechanism that enables context-aware calibration of perception uncertainty, leading to more accurate perception estimation. We further design a structured reward formulation that jointly considers perception, correctness, and task difficulty. In particular, an answer reward provides supervision for correctness, a perception- and difficulty-conditioned length reward adaptively regulates reasoning depth, and a perception reward encourages trajectories with stronger visual grounding. Extensive experiments on multiple multimodal reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that ThinkWise consistently improves the trade-off between accuracy and reasoning efficiency across both 3B and 7B models. These results highlight the importance of perception-aware reasoning and establish a principled framework for advancing LMRMs.

items.title: 3D Cell Morphology--Clinical Text Contrastive Learning with Voxel Swin Transformer and Finding Encoder Domain-Adaptation
items.description: Our prior work adapted a 2D CLIP dual encoder with LoRA to a multi-source cell-microscopy corpus, reaching anomaly-scoring ROC-AUC up to 0.985. This paper advances the same contrastive-learning domain-adaptation methodology from 2D microscope images to 3D microscope volumes, pairing a 3D Swin Transformer voxel encoder (MONAI's SwinUNETR backbone) with ClinicalBERT as the finding-text encoder. We train on 3,000 single-cell 3D confocal fluorescence volumes (4 tagged organelle structures) from the Allen Institute's public hiPSC single-cell image dataset, paired with template-generated finding text, with mitotic (dividing) cells oversampled as an abnormal-like proxy class validated by ROC-AUC. Naively reusing work's freeze backbone, LoRA the attention projections recipe for the Voxel Encoder collapses voxel embeddings to near-input-invariance, since LoRA's low-rank delta cannot compensate for an otherwise-frozen, randomly initialized (not pretrained) 3D Swin backbone, even as InfoNCE loss decreases healthily. Switching the Voxel Encoder to full fine-tuning resolves this: 4-way zero-shot structure accuracy rises from 25.0% (chance) to 48.6%, and voxel anomaly-scoring ROC-AUC improves from 0.486 to a peak of 0.628 (still below the 0.70 sanity threshold), while bidirectional retrieval recall stays low (R@10 $\le$3.8%). We further introduce a nearest-neighbor diagnosis-reason retrieval evaluation, reaching 29.8% hit-rate@{1,5} at its best scale while scoring 0.0% elsewhere. The central finding of this MVP is architectural: LoRA's parameter-efficiency assumption presumes a pretrained backbone worth preserving, and breaks down when the backbone is randomly initialized.

items.title: PACTHub: a large-scale structured experimental dataset for three-dimensional photoacoustic computed tomography
items.description: Three-dimensional photoacoustic computed tomography (PACT) provides volumetric contrast related to optical absorption for studying tissue anatomy and dynamics. Method development requires experimental datasets that retain measured signals and acquisition context. Public resources remain limited in their combined coverage of varied specimens, volumetric acquisition modes and reusable reconstruction information. Here we present PACTHub, a large-scale structured experimental dataset comprising 1,464 acquisition groups and 99,810 photoacoustic exposures collected over nearly four years. Animal, phantom and human measurements span single-position imaging, rotational compounding, panoramic scanning and time series. A common PAdata/JSON representation links acoustic signals to detector geometry, exposure selection, signal preparation and physical reconstruction coordinates. Public reconstruction implementations, numerical volumes and maximum-intensity projections provide practical entry points for reusing the measurements. Spatial and temporal examples demonstrate how retained acquisition relationships support panoramic reconstruction and regional signal analysis. Detector and exposure subsets enable studies of angular sampling and measurement budget. Volumetric evaluation combines PSNR, SSIM and L1 with Q, a complementary measure of local-contrast agreement within reference-defined structures. By connecting measured signals to reconstruction settings and numerical outputs, PACTHub makes its experimental scale and diversity available for reuse. It provides an experimental foundation for developing and evaluating artificial intelligence (AI) methods in volumetric PACT.

items.title: Perceptual Weight Space Programming for Diffusion Super-Resolution
items.description: Diffusion models for image super-resolution can recover scene content while producing distracting artifacts or unbalanced colors. We study whether a large language model (LLM) can improve perceptual quality by editing a small subset of existing U-Net weights without a clean reference image. The proposed framework provides the editor with architecture code, selected weights, activation summaries, and sampling previews. It permits up to 1,020 candidate trials while limiting accepted changes to three layers and fewer than 0.1\% of model parameters. The evaluation protocol uses ResShift, SinSR, and SUPIR and compares GPT-6 Astra with a specified Qwen3-VL model under matched access. Feedback metrics guide editing, while separate quality metrics and blinded human comparisons evaluate the final weights. We also report an executed color calibration experiment using real photographs and two small residual networks. This experiment demonstrates correction of a fixed color shift and reveals that an improving feedback score can accompany worse performance on unseen scenes. A separate lightweight super-resolution experiment isolates modest changes in luminance detail while preserving color. The findings motivate restricted updates and independent evaluation of perceptual weight editing.

items.title: Beyond Raw Similarity: Prior-Aware Fusion for Out-of-Distribution Detection
items.description: Out-of-distribution (OOD) detection in vision-language models presents unique challenges due to the reliance on cross-modal similarity. Even when embeddings are well separated for in-distribution (ID) data, similarity scores can remain overconfident for OOD inputs. A common remedy is to adapt the model on ID data, but adaptation discards the pretrained geometry that made the similarity meaningful. We propose multi-modal logit fusion (MM-Log), which keeps both by pairing a gradient-free zero-shot prior with a task-adapted branch in each modality and fuses their four cross-modal similarity channels into a single OOD score. Because the zero-shot priors are never adapted, the cross-channels act as a consistency check between the pretrained and adapted geometries: an OOD input that fools the adapted branch through a shortcut must additionally agree with frozen CLIP to retain a high score. We formalize this as a margin bound showing that the fused score is provably penalized by disagreement between the zero-shot and adapted branches, a signal to which adapted-only scores are structurally blind. MM-Log requires no auxiliary OOD data, negative prompts, or test-time adaptation, and trains on few-shot ID data alone. Across Far-OOD, Near-OOD, and Hard-OOD benchmarks, MM-Log consistently outperforms strong CLIP-based baselines.

items.title: ARC-VLN: Adaptive Recursive Computing-based Visual-Language Navigation
items.description: Efficient aerial visual-language navigation (VLN) requires reducing model storage and inference costs while maintaining instruction-conditioned action prediction. We present ARC-VLN, a token-type-aware recursive computation framework built on a language backbone with shared parameters. ARC-VLN retains full-depth computation for text and action tokens while adaptively selecting exit depths for visual tokens. Representations of early-exiting visual tokens are retained, and active-token compaction shortens the sequences processed by subsequent recursive blocks. To mitigate routing collapse to a single exit depth, we design a dedicated learning strategy that encourages the model to distribute visual tokens across multiple exit depths.On OpenFly's Test-Seen and Test-Unseen subsets, ARC-VLN achieves the lowest navigation error and the highest success rate and success weighted by path length among all compared methods. Meanwhile, it reduces the average number of decision steps per trajectory, total floating-point operations, mean model inference time per trajectory, and average GPU memory usage during inference, indicating its great potential as a VLN backbone for lightweight applications.

items.title: Where Does an On-Device Prescription Reader Lose Medications? A Frozen-Replay Study, from a 270M Language Model to a 2B Vision-Language Model
items.description: On-device models let a phone read a prescription without sending the photograph anywhere, but small models fail in ways that are hard to attribute: to the camera, the OCR, the model, or the rules around it. We study a phone-based pipeline that reads a prescription photograph with PaddleOCR, extracts medications with a 270M-parameter language model, and filters the result with a deterministic backstop before showing suggestions. Replaying identical frozen inputs through each configuration, with deterministic generation verified, we compare configurations with paired document-level intervals on 49 captures of 15 synthetic prescriptions (6 typed, 9 handwritten by one writer). Production recall is 8%, and 0 of 45 on handwriting. The backstop removes no correct medication and cuts unsafe outputs from 45 to 1. On handwriting nearly all medications never reach the model in readable form; on typed sheets the model mostly picks the wrong text. We trace much of the handwriting floor to a defect in our own crop step, then replace the pipeline: rotated-box crops, a 2B-parameter vision-language model that re-reads prescription lines and extracts the medications, and per-line numeric grounding. On the same captures recall rises from 8% to 67% (paired +59 points, 95% CI +40 to +78): typed 19% to 100%, handwritten 0 to 20 of 45, with no unsafe output. Rotated crops account for most of the reading gain and the model for most of the recall gain, and the OCR confidence gate is now the main limit. The cost is 61 s per photograph against about 12 s, and about 1.9 GB of memory. An earlier claim that better OCR lowered recall does not survive the controlled comparison, and we withdraw it. All results are in-sample, from one writer and one device.

items.title: What Does Hard-Negative Fine-Tuning Teach Multimodal Large Language Models? Controlled Evidence from a Compositional Benchmark
items.description: Fine-tuning on hard negatives is a popular way to improve the compositional reasoning of vision-language models, but when accuracy goes up it is rarely clear what the model actually learned. We ask this question for multimodal large language models. We use CompHall, 2,860 forced-choice questions (spatial, attribute, counting and part-whole) with two graded hard negatives each, three model families (LLaVA-1.5, LLaVA-NeXT and Idefics2), and controls that such studies often lack: gray-image evaluation, three seeds, option-order tests, control arms trained on different question types, and independent benchmarks. We find four things. First, CompHall is not a pure test of vision: part-whole questions can be answered from the text alone (66-95% without the image), and per-image accuracy is unrelated to an object-hallucination probe (r = -0.05), so we see no evidence that compositional failures drive hallucination. Second, the original fine-tuning method scored mostly image-placeholder tokens and hurt both LLaVA models. With a corrected loss, fine-tuning raises accuracy on the spatial-relation questions of CV-Bench in all three families, by +3.2, +23.1 and +6.0 points (averaged over both option orders). Control arms show that the gain needs spatial training questions, and for LLaVA-NeXT about two-thirds of it appears even on relation words that were only wrong options in training. Third, the gain is not general: on CompHall itself it is significant only for LLaVA-NeXT (+6.9 points) and not detectable for Idefics2, it reaches about 3 points at most on true/false statements, and LLaVA-1.5 fine-tuned on other question types learns to answer "true" too often. Fourth, both losses raise the yes-bias of LLaVA-1.5 on POPE.

items.title: Small Data in Long-Term Environmental Vision: Annotation Noise, Gamification, and Label-Budget Scaling
items.description: Long-running environmental camera networks produce abundant images but few reliable annotations. Using FujiView, a network of webcams around Mount Fuji, we study three linked questions: whether gamification affects annotation participation and agreement, how annotators disagree on ordinal visibility labels, and how label budget affects downstream classification. Across seven nonrandomized sessions with 22 labelers, gamification showed a more promising pattern for sustained participation than for labeling speed or agreement. In the closest remote-session comparison, the session recorded as gamified had longer active labeling time, while throughput and reference agreement remained similar. Annotation disagreement was substantial at fine granularity: crowd votes matched the single-annotator reference on 49.1% of exact visibility classes, versus 90.2% after grouping them into Good/Poor. In five-replicate label-budget experiments, models using 25% of the available label pool achieved held-out exact accuracy only 2.8 percentage points below the full-pool model on average. Together, these findings highlight the importance of designing reliable annotation targets, evaluating engagement mechanisms without assuming causal benefits, and using empirical scaling curves to plan labeling effort.

items.title: Different Timescales, Different Signals: Multimodal Landmark-Visibility Prediction in a Long-Term Webcam Network
items.description: Scenic visibility is not a single forecasting problem: planning a trip months ahead, deciding whether to go outside today, and judging whether tomorrow will be clear rely on different information. Using a year-scale multimodal archive of Mount Fuji webcams and meteorological observations, we identify a clear hierarchy across timescales. Seasonal climatology provides useful long-range guidance, webcam imagery is the strongest same-day observation (AUC 0.95), and the numerical forecast valid on the target day carries most of the day-specific signal one to three days ahead. Revealing this hierarchy requires evaluation that respects the dependence among cameras observing the same regional weather state: permissive splits substantially overstate multi-day performance, while date-grouped and forward-in-time evaluation reduce the apparent contribution of the current scene and current weather. On 6,575 camera-days, the current visual summary provides no measurable one-day gain once the target-day forecast is available. The remaining opportunity lies at shorter horizons, where the present visual representation discards cloud geometry and motion. These results recast scenic visibility prediction as a multi-timescale sensing problem rather than a single multimodal forecasting task.

items.title: Robustness as a Transferable Skill: Cross-Task Adversarial Defense for Vision-Language-Action Policies
items.description: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies are vulnerable to adversarial visual perturbations, while defenses often require task-specific adversarial fine-tuning. We investigate whether robustness learned on source manipulation tasks can protect independently specialized target policies without target-side adversarial training. We first show that even a single source defense update improves robustness on held-out tasks, establishing cross-task defense reuse independently of multi-source aggregation. To combine source updates, we introduce Source-Norm Transferable Robustness Vector (SN-TRV), which retains the direction of their mean while calibrating its magnitude using source-update norms. The resulting update is applied to the target visual encoder without target adversarial data, target-side gradient optimization, or additional inference modules. Evaluations across three VLA backbones, fixed and adaptive attacks, and different source defense recipes show improved robustness over naive averaging and identify limits in attack coverage. Physical PiPER trials increase average success under printed adversarial patches from 20.3% to 45.8%.

items.title: Technical Report of Auriga's 1:10 Scale Autonomous Vehicle Robot
items.description: This report presents the design and implementation of Auriga Robotics' 1:10 scale autonomous vehicle, developed at Shahid Beheshti University's Robotics and Intelligent Automation Laboratory. The platform integrates a custom mechanical chassis, a distributed embedded system based on ESP32 microcontrollers, and a Jetson Orin NX module for high-level perception and control. The embedded layer manages sensor interfacing, real-time data acquisition, and actuator control, while the Jetson handles environment perception through deep-learning--based lane, sign, and traffic light detection, as well as decision-making and trajectory control. System communication is achieved via structured UART links, ensuring synchronized operation between perception and control subsystems. The vehicle's software stack incorporates ROS, modular firmware design, and multiple control algorithms---Stanley, PID, and Pure Pursuit---to achieve stable autonomous navigation in structured driving scenarios. The overall system demonstrates robust performance and reliability in urban-like environments, serving as a modular research platform for future autonomous driving studies.

items.title: Passage-Focused Soft Coordination for Hierarchical Multi-Robot Navigation in Bottleneck Environments
items.description: In multi-robot navigation, rigid global schedules are sensitive to execution deviations, while local methods lack long-horizon coordination. We propose a passage-focused framework combining soft global coordination with flexible local execution. A passage-induced graph of convex sets supports priority-ordered planning with two levels of soft coordination. Passage-aware route selection accounts for passage usage and traversal directions, while route-restricted continuous space-time planning penalizes temporal conflicts. The resulting references guide a model predictive path integral controller that avoids collisions online. Adaptive temporal and geometric tracking accommodates execution deviations, while selective replanning maintains coordination without rigid trajectory reservations. Across 1,200 instances in 4 different environments with 5-30 robots, the framework achieves a near-perfect success rate and outperforms evaluated baselines in makespan and flowtime. Hardware experiments with 8 robots demonstrate successful completion of all trials without collisions. These results highlight the effectiveness of passage-focused coordination in balancing long-horizon cooperation with flexible execution.

items.title: Correcting Persistent Failures in Point-Cloud Grasping Policies using Human Demonstrations in Virtual Reality
items.description: Robots in homes, warehouses and farms must pick up objects they have never seen, usually without a 3D model or a category label. A grasping policy that works directly on the point cloud from a depth sensor needs only the geometry the robot observes, so it applies to any new object. Offline grasp generators such as Contact-GraspNet work this way, but they rank grasps by learned plausibility rather than by whether the grasp actually lifts the object. Reinforcement learning (RL) can optimize for that directly and make a point-cloud grasping policy much better on average, yet it leaves specific grasps persistently unsolved. We present a human-in-the-loop failure loop that targets those grasps: situations an RL policy keeps failing are mined automatically, sent to a virtual-reality application where a person picks the object up with their own hands, and returned to training as two grasp points. The person contributes only where to grasp; the robot chooses its own approach. In simulation, RL raises success on unseen objects from 55% with Contact-GraspNet to 83%. Adding 58 human demonstrations nearly doubles success on the hard cases RL kept failing, from 24% to 45%, and recovers performance that RL alone loses on similar cases that were never demonstrated, without reducing success on unseen objects.

items.title: Optimal Operating-Point Selection for Single-Linearization Trajectory Planning of Nonlinear Robot Manipulators
items.description: Single-point linearization provides a computationally efficient basis for optimization-based trajectory planning of nonlinear robot manipulators. However, planning performance depends on the selected linearization point. This paper presents an offline performance-driven approach that treats the location of a single linearization as an optimization variable. Candidate operating points are sampled from a common cubic seed trajectory, and each corresponding affine model is used to solve an identical constrained finite-horizon quadratic program (QP). The resulting control sequences are executed on the original nonlinear dynamics, and the operating point minimizing the nonlinear trajectory objective is selected through grid search and bounded refinement. Evaluation on four point-to-point motions of a three-degree-of-freedom UR5 manipulator yields optimal normalized operating-point locations between 0.325 and 0.935, demonstrating trajectory-dependent selection. Compared with the best-performing conventional initial, midpoint, or terminal linearization, the proposed approach reduces the nonlinear trajectory objective by 17-18%, 21-22%, 37-38%, and 7-8% across the four tasks, respectively. Additional nonlinear execution with identical PID feedback correction confirms that the performance advantage persists for a representative task. These results demonstrate that systematic operating-point selection can substantially improve single-linearization trajectory planning while preserving a fixed affine planning model.

items.title: TMA: Sim-to-Real Forceful Humanoid Manipulation via Tactile-Driven Motor Adaptation
items.description: Recent humanoid loco-manipulation in articulated environments has largely focused on geometry-dominant interactions, where success is primarily determined by geometric alignment and motion execution. In contrast, forceful multi-finger manipulation requires the robot to adapt to real-world uncertainties in contact and interaction dynamics. We present Tactile-Driven Motor Adaptation (TMA) and an integrated whole-body system for zero-shot sim-to-real forceful humanoid manipulation, and study round-doorknob opening as a challenging benchmark requiring stable multi-finger frictional grasping, sufficient torque generation without slip, force-regulated pushing, and whole-body stability. TMA structures policy learning around interactions observable through tactile feedback, uses cone geometry as an inductive bias for multi-finger contact representation, and adapts motor behavior online from tactile history. An upper-body manipulation policy is trained alongside a pretrained general locomotion controller to coordinate dexterous interaction and whole-body stabilization. Trained entirely in simulation, TMA transfers zero-shot to a Unitree G1 humanoid with BrainCo Revo2 multi-fingered hands and substantially outperforms standard Rapid Motor Adaptation (RMA) and reactive tactile policy baselines across four commercial round doorknobs in the real world.

items.title: Robot Demonstration Videos Should Include Transparency Disclosures
items.description: This paper argues that the robotics and AI community should adopt disclosure standards for demonstration videos. As physical and financial constraints limit direct public access to embodied AI, public dissemination of progress in robotics is mainly through curated demonstration videos rather than direct experience with the technology. In a large-scale (N=9,341), pre-registered experiment across six countries, we find that the general public struggles to discern both the visual authenticity (e.g., distinguishing real footage from CGI) and behavioral authenticity (e.g., distinguishing autonomy from teleoperation) of robot demonstration videos. The omission of these details distorts public perception, leading people to overestimate the ability of robots to perform tasks and navigate real world environments. Using evidence from behavioral science, we design a disclosure intervention and demonstrate that the inclusion of clear disclosures in robot demonstration videos significantly improves discernment of visual and behavioral authenticity, as well as understanding robots' capabilities. We propose the adoption of disclosure standards for robot demonstration videos to accurately calibrate public expectations and promote transparency in robotics research.

items.title: Refinement vs. Replanning: Inference Compute Allocation in Robot Policies
items.description: A frozen chunked robot policy can spend deployment-time inference compute in two coupled ways: more work within each policy call to refine a predicted action chunk, or more frequent policy calls to replan from fresh observations. We study this allocation without updating model weights. Our evaluation procedure reports success with both nominal compute rate and complete attempt cost, selects comparisons on discovery tasks, and tests prespecified comparisons on held-out tasks. Comparisons added after inspecting the held-out results only summarize observed patterns. We demonstrate the procedure with one frozen SmolVLA checkpoint in synchronous LIBERO simulation, using denoising count as the refinement control and fixing chunk length at K=50. Arithmetic and latency characterize cost differently: at d=10, 82.1% of counted arithmetic is independent of denoising, whereas a descriptive affine fit to fixed-input host time assigns 17.7% to its intercept. At h=2, d=2 succeeds on 139/160 attempts versus 122/160 for d=5 (+10.6 percentage points; task-conditional 95% interval: +4.4 to +16.9), while using 5.9% less arithmetic per control step. Executing h=5 rather than h=2 at d=2 yields 138/160 versus 139/160 successes and 60.7% lower arithmetic per attempt; equivalence is not established. The case study shows why deployment adaptation must evaluate generation effort and feedback frequency jointly; it does not define a universal setting.

items.title: Certify, Then Select: Viability-Aware Runtime Steering of Frozen Diffusion Policies
items.description: Diffusion policies, which generate short action sequences by denoising random noise, are a leading way to learn robot skills from demonstrations. Once deployed, they meet constraints the demonstrations never contained, and retraining for each is impractical. A safety filter edits the policy's action to satisfy them, but the edit ignores the task, and a large edit can leave the policy where it cannot continue. We propose CAST (Certified Action Selection at Test time): draw a few action chunks from the frozen policy, certify each with a barrier condition, and execute the certified chunk that a learned value ensemble ranks highest. We prove that a certified step is safe whatever the critic does; that, whenever a certified sample exists, the executed chunk stays within log N nats of the policy conditioned on feasibility, while a safety-filter projection can be singular to it; and that an exact closed-loop identity splits the gain of ranking into availability, spread and the critic's target. Certifying the next chunk is not enough: a generative controller can have safe actions available now and none later. We characterise the safe control authority of a frozen policy under finite sampling, and CAST-V preserves it through a policy-conditioned viability, estimated with a model under a finite-sample guarantee or learned from the controller's own logs (CAST-VL). On robomimic manipulation, a planar quadrotor, a MuJoCo humanoid and a unicycle, with frozen policies, CAST raises joint task-and-constraint success above the output filter in nearly every setting; certifying before ranking is decisive where a filter's edit is large, and viability removes most dead ends that one-step certification cannot see. Project page: https://clmoro.github.io/cast.

items.title: RoboCoEvo: Expanding Robot Capabilities through Agent-Policy Co-Evolution
items.description: Integrating MLLM-based agents with robotic foundation models has attracted increasing attention as a means of enhancing robotic capabilities. However, the improvement of such integrated systems remains largely decoupled across their agent and model components, with advances in one component not necessarily benefiting the other, substantially limiting the capabilities of the combined system. As both MLLMs and robotic foundation models become increasingly capable, fully realizing their combined potential calls for co-evolution, an iterative process in which improvements in agents and robotic foundation models reinforce one another. We propose RoboCoEvo, a failure-guided co-evolution framework that couples the refinement of the agent's explicit and reusable executable knowledge with parameter learning in robotic foundation models, such as vision-language-action (VLA) models. Through a code-as-policy formulation, the agent develops and refines executable failure-detection and recovery programs, generating targeted corrective experience. Post-training consolidates the resulting corrective behaviors into the robotic model's end-to-end policy, improving autonomous task execution. Changes in the updated policy's failure distribution, in turn, guide subsequent revisions to the agent's programs. Experiments on BEHAVIOR-1K, RoboCasa, and RoboTwin demonstrate sustained improvements in autonomous VLA task performance across successive co-evolution rounds.

items.title: Leaning Over to Reach Far-Away Objects
items.description: We study supported reaching to extend a humanoid robot's workspace by bracing against the environment for stabilization using a straightforward yet capable whole-body model predictive control (MPC) approach, exclusively with local sensing and fiducial markers. While typical solutions for whole body humanoid control aim at avoiding or accommodating contact, contact is explicitly required to reach objects placed on surfaces far out of normal reach. We employ sampling-based MPC for whole-body leaning, bracing, reaching, and recovery on a Unitree H1-2 humanoid. The controller runs in real-time at 34 Hz on a laptop, transfers sim-to-real, extends reach by about 50 cm beyond the unbraced standing workspace, and sustains the loaded posture for over four minutes, before pose estimation drifts. The controller reaches the commanded target in 89% of trials and completes the full reach-and-recovery cycle in 81%, across 54 trials spanning six targets and three table heights. We further characterize why such a small real-time sampling budget is sufficient, finding that temporal persistence of sampled actions and exploration scale strongly govern success, while CEM provides the widest operating region over planning rate and model mismatch. These results establish a real-world baseline for online, contact-rich humanoid manipulation. Code, videos, and full hardware details are available at https://h12leaner.github.io/

items.title: Wireless Edge-Assisted Adaptive Latent Reasoning for Vision-Language-Action Models in Physical AI
items.description: Vision-language-action (VLA) models enable embodied artificial intelligence (AI) by translating visual observations and language instructions into robotic actions. Emerging use cases in physical AI are expected to drive the need for efficient inference and communication, as the computational demands of the VLA models pose challenges for real-time control with limited onboard resources. Test-time scaling through latent reasoning allows these models to refine hidden representations without generating explicit chain-of-thought (CoT) tokens, but introduces a trade-off between task success, inference latency, and energy consumption. In this paper, we address the efficient collaborative inference under a realistic communication scenario. We propose a wireless edge-assisted framework for adaptive latent reasoning (WEALR) that augments onboard computation with edge computing. A decision-making agent jointly selects the execution location and latent-reasoning convergence threshold. We formulate this joint adaptation as a constrained Markov decision process (CMDP). A Lagrangian-constrained deep reinforcement learning (CDRL) approach, namely trust region policy optimization Lagrangian (TRPO-Lag), learns to balance task performance and resource consumption under varying wireless conditions and task requirements. We evaluate the framework using LIBERO manipulation tasks, profiled VLA inference costs, and ray-traced wireless channels. Experimental results demonstrate that TRPO-Lag achieves up to 23% higher feasibility-weighted task success rate compared to benchmark CDRL methods.

items.title: SuperGlance: Driving at a Glance with a Vision-Language Model
items.description: Autonomous driving is turning to vision-language-action models (VLAs). They answer and plan by decoding, one step at a time. Each step is another forward pass, so a plan can take over a second of GPU time. Embodied AI often pairs such a slow, reasoning System 2 with a fast System 1 that acts. Human drivers plan at a glance, with System 1. Faster designs usually put System 1 outside the vision-language model (VLM), in a planner without its abilities. Yet before a VLM writes its first token, it has already read the scene into one hidden state. We show that, once trained, this hidden state is enough to drive and to answer questions about what the model sees. SuperGlance reads it to turn a decoder-only VLM into an encoder-style driving policy. Its linear head scores a fixed set of 5,273 candidate trajectories. With the set fixed, rewards are computed offline, so supervised targets can be reward-weighted and reinforcement learning maximizes the exact expected reward. Before and during policy training, multiple-choice training keeps the VLM's visual abilities in one pass, so the policy still answers questions about driving scenes. Training questions are built against shortcuts. Each must be answered right in two option orders. Against drift, a KL term keeps each stage near its starting model. One pass offers VLAs a more plausible path to System 1. SuperGlance answers visual multiple-choice questions as well as its base VLM does by decoding. It plans in 84 ms of GPU time, six times faster than Qwen-Drive-1.0, and at least as well on NAVSIM, PAI-AV and WOD-E2E. In AlpaSim closed loop, km per at-fault incident holds for both planners up to a 300-ms delay and drops beyond. With GPU time charged as delay, SuperGlance's lead over Qwen-Drive-1.0 grows from 2.8 to 3.9 times. Delayed by 1.2 s, our model falls below Qwen-Drive-1.0 at its own 518 ms.

items.title: ImpedanceMimic: Learned Impedance as Action Space for Force-Accurate Motion Imitation
items.description: Recovering the forces behind a motion is ill-posed: different controllers can reproduce the same movement while generating different contact forces. Physics-based motion imitation resolves this ambiguity through simulation, but relies on fixed-gain proportional-derivative (PD) control. We show that fixed gains impose a trade-off between motion and force tracking, as contact and swing place conflicting demands on joint stiffness and damping. We introduce ImpedanceMimic, a reinforcement-learning policy that modulates per-joint stiffness, damping, and position setpoints from motion and force measurements, but requires only motion at inference. Across 129 participants and six activities, ImpedanceMimic outperforms matched fixed-gain PD under every integration scheme, direct-torque, muscle-actuated and existing imitation controllers in kinematic and force fidelity, approaching a dedicated motion-to-force regressor. By expressing gains as multiples of inertia-scaled priors, a single policy controls subject-specific biomechanical models without explicit anthropometric input and transfers zero-shot to unseen humans and a humanoid robot. The learned impedance forms a low-dimensional representation of motor state, shared across bodies, that generalizes to withheld activities: stiffness scales with load, and damping anticipates unloading.

items.title: Distilling Safety Filters for Filter-free Multi-agent RL
items.description: Reinforcement learning (RL) can teach robot teams to navigate shared spaces, but trial and error causes collisions that real robots cannot afford. Control barrier function (CBF) safety filters prevent these collisions by correcting unsafe actions, yet in a team the filter becomes a centralized optimization whose number of constraints grows quadratically with the team size. We propose an approach that builds the filter's safety into the RL policy and examine how such a system behaves during filter-free deployment. However, the filter that keeps training safe also hides what the policy must learn: it masks the cost of unsafe actions, which actor-critic methods then overvalue, and it keeps near-collision states out of the training data. Our approach therefore learns only from executed safe actions with implicit Q-learning and distills the filter into the policy at synthetic near-collision states. We prove that filter distillation loss bounds the policy's constraint violation and hence how far agents can cross their safety margin, so errors never accumulate. When distillation states cover deployed states, the loss also bounds the collision probability at every step. Without a filter and acting only on local observations, our policies have no collisions in 1,800 test episodes with multiple agents. A policy trained with three agents transfers zero-shot to teams of twenty at constant per-agent computation and stays collision-free with up to eight agents. We test our policies on Crazyflie quadrotors with up to five flying at the same time.

items.title: Ego2Sim2Humanoid: Agentic Real-to-Sim for Learning Loco-Manipulation VLAs without Robot Demonstrations
items.description: Imitation learning for visuomotor policies typically relies on teleoperated robot demonstrations, which are costly because every episode requires a trained operator controlling a physical robot in real time through teleoperation interfaces and wearable body-tracking hardware. Egocentric glasses capture human demonstrations without a robot or handheld grippers, yet they track only the head and in-view human hands, and directly copying human motion to a robot with different stature, arm reach and hand morphology fails to produce feasible contacts. \method{} converts egocentric glasses recordings into physically verified robot training trajectories. An agentic real-to-sim stage reconstructs collision and textured visual assets from the recorded RGB-D and head streams, completes unseen surfaces when needed, and predicts target contact bands on the manipulated objects. During motion adaptation, a grasp planner turns each contact band into a feasible robot wrist pose and finger closure, bilevel stance optimization plans collision-free standing postures that keep hand targets reachable, and a whole-body motion generator synthesizes lower-body locomotion and out-of-view arm motion. Two-stage motion correction then blends visibility transitions kinematically and trains a reinforcement-learning tracking policy in physics simulation under agent-designed semantic rewards, completing manipulation phases even when the object leaves the camera view. Rendering the reconstructed scene through the robot's onboard camera along the optimized rollout yields synchronized robot-view images, proprioception and verified action labels. Fine-tuned exclusively on this converted dataset, without real-robot demonstrations, GR00T N1.7 performed loco-manipulation tasks autonomously on a Unitree G1. Project page: https://robonana.github.io/ego2sim2humanoid/

items.title: Self-Calibrating Vision-Agent-Action: Deploying Pick-and-Place to New Robot Cells without Demonstrations or Fine-Tuning
items.description: In simulation, Vision-Agent-Action (VAA) performs pick-and-place in robot cells with gripper or base-frame changes without robot demonstrations or fine-tuning. It uses pre-trained vision-language and language models for interpretation, measures the command map and camera geometry from its own motion and fingertips, estimates lens distortion, and plans grasps from measured object depth. A controlled study of eight public LIBERO-fine-tuned vision-language-action models (VLAs) varies robot hardware, camera geometry, appearance, and base frame. Gripper and frame changes dominate their losses in the tested fractional design. Across 18 cells with these changes, frozen VAA achieves 230/360 successes (64%), the refined VAA 268/360 (74%), and the strongest released VLA on this subset 76/360 (21%). Paired ablations support the self-calibration bundle, lens estimation under compounded changes, and the measured-depth pipeline. On a two-step LIBERO-Goal chain with object state carried between instructions, VAA completes 54/60 chains in changed cells, while four evaluated VLAs complete none.

items.title: Continuous Lower-Limb Joint-Angle Estimation from sEMG and IMU: The Conditional Value of Cross-Activity and Cross-Subject Data under Update-Matched Controls
items.description: Intent-driven exoskeleton control needs a continuous, causal estimate of the wearer's joint kinematics and an answer to a second question: whose data should train the estimator for a new user? Borrowing the user's recordings of other activities, or other users' recordings of the same activity, is usually evaluated as "more data" versus "less data," which confounds the information a source carries with the optimizer updates it adds and hides negative transfer behind averages. We separate these effects for hip, knee, and ankle angle estimation from high-density sEMG and an IMU across six locomotion activities on all ten participants of a public dataset. A compact residual causal TCN-GRU decoder is frozen, and an update-matched replay control prices every added source against the same number of updates on the user's own data. A user's own other activities raise $R^2$ from 0.722 to 0.788, of which +0.048 is information beyond replay; stair descent is a reliably harmful donor and sit-stand-walk a reliably beneficial one. Other users' same-activity data help while the user has only the target activity ($G_\mathrm{T} = +0.053$) and half as much once own other-activity data exist ($G_\mathrm{W} = +0.028$); at full calibration, donor value collapses after one to two target records. Per-target gains from the two sources correlate, and leave-one-participant-out gates recover most of the cross-subject value only at low calibration. Data value is hierarchical, state-dependent, and directional; the bottleneck is deciding, without test labels, when to transfer.

items.title: Physics-Informed Causal Reasoning for Nonstationary Robot Dynamics
items.description: Reasoning about what an action will cause requires internalizing how a system behaves. As conditions seldom stay fixed, this must often happen within a few interactions. Yet systems that look identical in a snapshot can respond differently to the same action, depending on physical conditions the snapshot hides. Context-based models capture this separation by summarizing recent transitions into a latent context, but do not specify how that context should change the equations of motion. Physics-informed neural networks build those equations into the model, but describe only a single system and cannot recognize when it has changed. We present Physics-Informed Causal Reasoning (PICR), which bridges the two. Only a context, re-inferred from recent interactions, is updated; it conditions a fixed physics-informed network that determines the robot's inertia and potential energy, so the robot adapts to new physical conditions from its own experience without retraining or a hand-specified robot model. On a Franka Panda arm in NVIDIA Isaac Sim, PICR predicts motion under changing and unseen payloads, reducing error on the latter by 1.6-3.8x over baselines, and extends to counterfactual queries under alternative torques. Our analysis shows that the context, inferred solely from interaction, encodes payload physical properties, tracks their changes, and governs the arm's response. The gravity and inertia terms induced by the context further demonstrate its physical validity, each agreeing with the simulator at the level of individual Lagrangian components.

items.title: HospitalBench: Diagnosing Where and Why Embodied Agents Fail on Long Hospital Task Chains
items.description: Long-horizon embodied tasks fail in ways that end-task success cannot see. HospitalBench is a diagnostic benchmark of ten hospital chores in NVIDIA Isaac Sim, each two unscored warm-up steps followed by a causal chain of five scored sub-tasks in one continuous simulation: the state one step leaves (an object pose, a choice, a fact seen once) determines what the next step must do, unlike benchmarks that place sub-tasks side by side. Vision-language agents act through skill-level tools from camera images. A scripted robot that makes only the calls a model gets is the solvability check of a chore. From each trajectory the benchmark reads where a chain breaks, what the agent did after a failed call, and how far its own position estimate drifts from the true one. This version reports first results only: 15 of 60 planned runs (three models at high effort, one run each on chores T1 and T10 from both start states and T3 from one), with scripted-robot proofs on three of the ten chores. Of the 15 runs, 2 passed all five sub-tasks. Runs still going after sub-tasks 1 to 5 were 15, 8, 4, 2, 2. Of 189 failed calls, 168 were followed by a different call and 111 by a call that did not fail. These are first results and not a full benchmark. We will release the scenes, task chains, scripted robot, evaluation harness and trajectories.

items.title: VLN-Flash: Parallel Action Decoding with Adaptive Execution for Vision-and-Language Navigation
items.description: When a vision-and-language navigation policy generates an action sequence autoregressively, the robot waits for a chain of dependent predictions. A small discrete action vocabulary makes it possible to score all short-horizon plans in parallel. We introduce VLN-Flash, a training-free decoder that evaluates the complete action-prefix tree in a single forward pass. Branch-specific attention and matched token positions preserve the original policy's conditional action distribution for each prefix in exact arithmetic. We use the score margin between the stepwise-greedy prefix and its strongest alternative at each depth to decide how many actions to execute. The robot then executes the plan with the highest joint score at the chosen depth before observing again. On matched inputs, VLN-Flash achieves a nearly $3\times$ speedup in action decoding over native autoregression on Uni-NaVid and StreamVLN. Compared with the native autoregressive decoders, it improves success rate and success weighted by path length (SPL) on R2R-CE and RxR-CE, with success gains up to 2.7 percentage points. On a Unitree GO2, VLN-Flash improves navigation success and cuts the mean wait between actions by about 160 ms after subtracting network transmission time.

items.title: Residual Reinforcement Learning for Visual Servo Control with Zero-Shot Sim-to-Real Transfer
items.description: We address tracking a moving object on a conveyor with a Franka Emika Panda robot arm, despite an imprecise digital twin, measurement errors, and noise. Our novel approach augments a loop-shaped inverse-Jacobian PI controller with a residual policy learned via Soft Actor-Critic in the digital twin. A delay-compensated Kalman filter fuses out-of-sequence camera measurements to provide latency-aware moving target position estimates. We compare the achieved performance to a performance bound for a class of model-based controllers derived from a frequency-domain sensitivity analysis, quantifying the minimum achievable error imposed by uncertain kinematic model mismatch. Simulation and hardware experiments indicate that our residual policy drives tracking error below the bound. Across conveyor speeds (27.9-41.8 mm/s), our method reduces mean tracking errors from 1.1-1.4 mm (baseline inverse-Jacobian PI) to 0.3-0.7 mm. These results show that learning residual corrections in a limited-fidelity simulator, combined with delay compensation, can substantially improve model-based control under modeling and measurement uncertainties while maintaining reliable sim-to-real transfer.

items.title: MARS: Dynamic Routing of Reinforcement-Learned Atomic Skills for Multi-Stage Robotic Manipulation
items.description: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have demonstrated strong capabilities in multi-task robotic manipulation. However, they still face limitations in control precision and execution stability during critical manipulation stages, such as object grasping, alignment and insertion. To combine general-purpose manipulation capabilities with task-specific fine-grained control, while enabling effective coordination between generalist and specialized policies throughout multi-stage manipulation tasks, this paper proposes MARS (Modular Atomic-skill Routing System), a dynamic routing framework for reinforcement learning-based atomic skills. MARS integrates a frozen generalist VLA policy with multiple independently trained atomic skill policies. Using a shared RL Token state representation and the reference action of VLA, specialized control policies are optimized through reinforcement learning for different cr`itical manipulation stages. For high-level policy selection, we develop a dynamic router that integrates temporal context and skill semantics. The router employs Mamba-based recurrent encoding and a historical feature window to capture state evolution during manipulation. Skill descriptions of candidate policies are encoded into semantic queries, and attention mechanisms are used to establish correspondences between skill semantics and temporal state features. Experimental results show that MARS achieves an average Macro-F1 score of 90.47% across four LIBERO task suites under fixed-trajectory evaluation, outperforming an MLP-based router by 7.08 percentage points. In the simulated Tube Transport task, the full-task success rate increases from 20.04% to 85.67%. These results demonstrate that stage-specific reinforcement learning and temporal state-aware dynamic policy routing can improve multi-policy coordination and overall task execution performance in multi-stage robotic manipulation.

items.title: Long-Horizon Causal Inertial Odometry in Multistory Buildings
items.description: In indoor 3D localization inside multistory buildings, an elevator or an escalator accelerates for a few seconds and then cruises at constant velocity for tens of seconds. Gait excitation disappears, the specific force degenerates into a constant gravity reaction, and instantaneous velocity becomes unobservable within a 1-2 s window. The output of short-window learned inertial odometry consequently degrades toward the conditional mean of the training set, and vertical displacement is systematically underestimated. We propose Local-Token Causal Attention (LTCA), a long-horizon architecture that compresses each 1 s inertial window into a 1 Hz motion token and sustains, over a bounded 60 s causal cache, the motion state established at the onset event. We further introduce a pluggable barometer branch that, when online, supplies a direct elevation constraint to the vertical channel through local differential height observations, and we train it with paired online/fallback conditional training so that the barometer also regularizes the representation shared by the two modes during training. On MSIO, our benchmark of nine buildings, the RoNIN and TLIO instances reach 3D trajectory errors (ATE-3D) of 2.83/4.18 m and 2.44/5.12 m on the Seen and Unseen splits, respectively, with the barometer online. With the barometer disabled at inference, the same weights fall back to pure inertial inference and reach 3.24/4.28 m and 2.64/5.23 m, still below every native short-window baseline. We further validate the framework on the public RoNIN and TLIO benchmarks.

items.title: Energy-Based Reasoners: Your Recurrent Reasoner Should Be an Energy-Based Model
items.description: Looping is a powerful inductive bias for reasoning. By repeatedly iterating a recurrent block, looped models can scale their effective depth and enable multi-step reasoning in latent space. However, existing looped models are not inherently guided by an explicit measure of progress, making it difficult to determine when to stop looping and how to improve upon the current state. To enable this, we introduce Energy-Based Reasoners (EBRs), which learn an energy function over latent reasoning states and formulate looped updates as gradient descent on this energy. The energy scores latent states, while its gradient guides refinement and provides a signal for stopping. To train EBRs effectively, we further introduce exploration-based training to discover additional modes and to better shape the energy landscape over a broader set of states. Across four algorithmic reasoning benchmarks, EBRs match or outperform prior recurrent reasoning models, achieving 99.9% accuracy on Sudoku-Extreme while using 345times less inference compute than the next-best model and maintaining comparable training compute. On all multi-solution benchmarks, EBRs achieve state-of-the-art coverage of distinct valid solutions while maintaining near-100% single-sample accuracy. These results suggest that energy-based models are a promising approach for strong reasoning performance.

items.title: Flexible Multi-Stack Super-Resolution of Clinical Brain MRI Using Hetero-Orientation Variational Encoding: Expert Reader Evaluation in a Nigerian Cohort
items.description: High-resolution brain MRI is important for neuroradiological assessment, yet routine clinical protocols often rely on fast, anisotropic 2D acquisitions, particularly in resource-constrained settings. These acquisitions may differ in orientation, alignment and anatomical coverage, resulting in partially overlapping image stacks. Existing learning-based super-resolution methods typically rely on single, under-constrained inputs or fixed multi-stack configurations with idealised acquisition geometry. We introduce MS-HVED, a sequence-agnostic framework for flexible multi-stack brain MRI super-resolution. Available axial, coronal and sagittal stacks are independently encoded into multi-scale Gaussian posteriors and fused using a field-of-view-aware Product-of-Gaussians formulation that limits contributions from unsupported regions. Physics-informed domain randomisation simulates heterogeneous clinical acquisition conditions, including obliqueness, partial coverage and imaging artefacts.
